title: Organ flue pipe
reference_instrument: a different pipe, with a count: a 16 ft Principal at St. Jakobus, Ilmenau (MusicSphere Part 3, key B5, Mic 2, take 2, CC BY 4.0), ruled by the same key's other two takes and the neighbouring key C6. That organ's B sits at a' about 430 Hz, 39.1 c under A440, and the pitch is counted against the recording as measured
summary: One note, B4, on one measured tin flue pipe, graded against a recording of a different pipe: 1 of 14 measures, the partial frequencies, sits inside the spread between that pipe's own takes and its neighbouring key, and the same 1 on the same-note ruler. It speaks the right mode, but it is far too clean, still hollow and slow to speak, and before it settles it plays a tone the real pipe doesn't have. The pipe comes from Castellengo's 2004 measurements and is blown at its measured 360 Pa through the paper's short attack. The jet isn't this pipe's own: its spreading law is a trial from Fletcher's 1976 E4 pipe, its 0.666 mm labium offset is carried from the same pipe, and the limit on its swing is Fletcher's envelope with timing set by this model. It holds 492.8 Hz, +64 c against the pipe's measured first resonance; before the open end was unflanged it held 488.7 Hz (+49 c), about 40 c of that the passive network's own on one reading of the paper's length.
physics_present: fs-couple flue_loop on the generic flue network route (music_render wind): a jet driven by the foot pressure acting on a connected duct network, the route the recorder, tin whistle and pan pipes use, with no organ-shaped code
The measured pipe (Castellengo, ISMA 2004): 27 mm bore, 308.5 mm from mouth centre to open end, a mouth 21 mm wide with a 7 mm cut-up, and a 0.25 mm flue
The measured wind: 360 Pa, reached by the paper's short attack (125 Pa at 9 ms, 360 Pa at 45 ms)

The mouth's acoustic mass from its own 3-D wall cut, and radiation from the mouth (its memory stepped exactly with the flow held over each step, 27631e7a4) and open end, the open end pushing back on the bore as an unflanged pipe end (Garcia Mayen 2021, Eq. 14, with Silva et al. 2009, Eqs. 10-11; ae3ef2d4e) and heard as baffled
Dry room air at 20 C, fractional-delay propagation and gas-derived viscothermal loss on the bore (its memory stepped exactly with the flow held over each step, adbb97dbb and f78078db2)

A forced Bickley jet, spreading by Fletcher 1976's organ-flue Pitot law. That's a trial here: it was measured on an E4 pipe with flues of 0.25 to 1.0 mm, so this flue is in range, but it isn't this pipe

A labium offset of 0.666 mm (2.66 flue heights). It isn't a measurement of this pipe: it carries Fletcher's voicing b0 of about -0.4, printed for Fletcher's perspex E4 pipe, through Fletcher's jet width at this cut-up
A limit on how far the jet can swing: Fletcher 1976's envelope, with no coefficient to set. The way it's applied in time is this model's: the gain changes only when the jet changes sign
The first mode: it speaks 492.8 Hz from about 0.14 s on

Room air on the way to the microphone: the receiver hears the pipe through the exterior air's viscous and thermal absorption on every path from the open end and the mouth (`observer_gas stokes-kirchhoff`, on the flue route since da45542bd), as the flute and whistle pages do. It changes the sound on its way, not the pipe: the held note moves by less than 0.01 c, and on the comparison with the different pipe's recording the same measures as before sit inside the spread between that pipe's takes
physics_missing: A recording of this pipe: the graded clip is a 16 ft Principal at St. Jakobus, Ilmenau, key B5, sounding 482.85 Hz, so the count is against a different pipe, and nothing about it went into the card. Its pitch counts as measured: this pipe sounds 35.2 c above it, outside the spread, on an organ whose B sits 39.1 c under A440 (a' about 430 Hz)

Noise: the harmonics-to-noise gap to the recording is 56.8 dB. The card has no jet noise: that row's gate opens at a flue Reynolds number of 700, and this flue runs near 400. The real pipe's floor may also come from its blower, valve or room. A resolved 3-D slot-jet run at about this flue's Reynolds number (410, cut-up 28 jet heights), made to see whether the jet turns broadband, refused itself early in its settling: the lattice stopped on a non-positive density at the inlet end (x = 3), so this pipe has no jet noise from resolved turbulence yet
Even harmonics: odd stand +1.9 dB over even, against -10.9 dB in the recording. H2 is still about 14 dB under even the two lower microphones on the real pipe, and it leans on the borrowed offset
Prompt speech: the attack takes 228 ms, 10 to 90 %, against 16.6 ms. The card's ramp reaches 360 Pa at 45 ms, so it isn't the ramp, and the cause is unexplained
The right first sound: a tone near 1530 Hz, the pipe's third mode, leads from 20 to 120 ms. The recording opens on its own second harmonic at 966 Hz
The high harmonics: H5 to H11 sit 4 to 33 dB under the recording, all above 2 kHz, where the compact receiver on this route isn't valid, so it may not all be the jet

A jet at a real pipe's swing: its swing is still 13 flue heights, where de la Cuadra 2005 records a free jet at 3.3 to 3.95. A jet card measured on a rig fed by blowing pressure was tried in place of the interim one and refused itself. At Re about 148 the rig's tone locks at 0.31 to 0.79 times Brown's stage-I edge-tone law and moves 52 % when the rig is a quarter longer. With an absorbing layer at the outlet the two lengths lock within 9 % of each other, but the jet slows to Re about 93 and locks at 0.62 to 0.68 times the law. No cause is named

Pitch: the held note is +64 c against the pipe's measured first resonance of 475 Hz. Before the open end was unflanged, about 40 c of the then +49 c was the passive network's own 486 Hz with the length read from the languid, and that network has not been re-read with the unflanged end. The paper doesn't say where its 312 mm is measured from, and the upper-lip reading gives 476 Hz. On the card without the swing limit, the pitch also moved with a numerical setting

This pipe's own voicing, and what the paper doesn't state: the wall thickness, the point the length is measured from, the upper lip, the flattened mouth, the flue's depth, the languid, the foot, the toe hole and the room
Mouth tones, chiff and wind noise of the attack. The route has no hydrodynamic feedback from the labium to the flue and no resolved jet, so it can't make edge tones

Separated flow at the open end: the flow leaving the open end separates and loses its kinetic energy, a loss in series with the end's own radiation (`opening_losses`, Δp = ρQ|Q|/(2(C_c A)²)). Tried with C_c 1, the open end as Atig, Dalmont and Gilbert 2004 print it (C. R. Mécanique 332:299-304, Eq. 3, c_d = 2 for a thin-walled unflanged end), once the solver took a pressure drop or power too small for double precision as the zero it rounds to (the first try was refused on such a step): the note rises 0.44 c on a refined peak and 0.27 c on zero crossings (the grader's 492.76 to 492.90 Hz, a pitch gap to the recording of 35.17 to 35.65 c) and plays 0.9 dB quieter. Of the grader's measures against the recording of a different pipe, 10 move nearer, the most harmonics-to-noise (56.76 to 55.69 dB) and partial trajectories (20.23 to 19.56 dB), and 3 move further: pitch, odd/even balance (12.81 to 13.04 dB) and partial frequencies (0.05 to 0.09 c, past the 0.08 c spread between takes), so 1 of 15 measures sits inside that spread, against 2 without the row. The page keeps the end without the loss
